# NodeMCU (ESP8266) — pin/boot/function reference (straight to the point)

Nice — here’s a clear, no-fluff rundown of NodeMCU (ESP8266/ESP-12E style) pins, what they map to, what they do, and the important gotchas so your project doesn’t brick at boot.

## Quick pin map (common NodeMCU board labels → ESP8266 GPIO)
| NodeMCU label | ESP GPIO | Common use / note |
|---:|---:|---|
| D0 | GPIO16 | Wake/Deep-sleep wake. **No** PWM, no I2C, limited features. |
| D1 | GPIO5  | Often used as **SCL (I2C)**. PWM/interrupts ok. |
| D2 | GPIO4  | Often used as **SDA (I2C)**. PWM/interrupts ok. |
| D3 | GPIO0  | **BOOT**: must be **HIGH** for normal run; LOW enters flash mode. Has internal pull-up. |
| D4 | GPIO2  | Onboard LED on many boards (inverted). Must be **HIGH** at boot. |
| D5 | GPIO14 | SPI SCLK (HSPI), used for SPI, PWM ok. |
| D6 | GPIO12 | SPI MISO (HSPI), PWM ok. |
| D7 | GPIO13 | SPI MOSI (HSPI), PWM ok. |
| D8 | GPIO15 | SPI CS / boot strap: must be **LOW** at boot. |
| RX  | GPIO3  | U0RX (Serial RX). |
| TX  | GPIO1  | U0TX (Serial TX). |
| A0  | ADC0   | Analog input. On NodeMCU mapped to **0–3.3V** (board adds divider); raw ESP8266 ADC is 0–1.0V. |
| 3V3 | —      | 3.3V output/regulator — power device from here (limited current). |
| GND | —      | Ground. |
| VIN / VU / 5V | — | On some boards `VIN` or `VU` is USB 5V or raw input to regulator. |

## SPI and I²C defaults
- **SPI (HSPI)** default pins:  
  SCLK = D5 (GPIO14), MISO = D6 (GPIO12), MOSI = D7 (GPIO13), CS = D8 (GPIO15).  
- **I²C default pins** (in Arduino core/NodeMCU examples): SDA = D2 (GPIO4), SCL = D1 (GPIO5).  
  — Both I2C and SPI can be remapped in software to other pins if needed.

## UARTs
- **UART0**: TX = GPIO1 (TX), RX = GPIO3 (RX). Used for programming & serial logging. Be careful if driving these.
- **UART1**: TX only (GPIO2) — used for debug prints sometimes.

## PWM, interrupts, and other features
- Most GPIOs (except GPIO16/D0) support PWM, interrupts, and `digitalWrite`/`digitalRead`.
- GPIO16 (D0) does not support `attachInterrupt()` in the same way and has limitations (used for deep sleep wake).

## Boot-mode strapping pins — critical
At reset the values on these pins determine boot mode. Messing these up will stop the board from starting normally:
- **GPIO0 (D3)** — should be **HIGH** for normal boot; **LOW** for flash mode.
- **GPIO2 (D4)** — must be **HIGH** on boot.
- **GPIO15 (D8)** — must be **LOW** on boot.

If you connect external circuits that pull these pins to wrong levels during reset (e.g., LEDs, sensors, relays), the board may fail to boot. **Rule of thumb:** don’t attach outputs or pull these pins to the opposite levels unless you handle boot-time state.

## Pins to avoid or be cautious with
- **GPIO9 & GPIO10** — connected to flash memory on many modules (ESP-12 variants). Don’t use them unless you know what you’re doing.
- **D3/D4 (GPIO0/2)** and **D8 (GPIO15)** — watch boot strapping rules (see above).
- **Serial TX/RX (GPIO1, GPIO3)** — don’t tie heavy loads to them; they’re used for programming and serial monitor.
- **Powering heavy loads** (motors, large sensors) from 3.3V regulator on the board can reset it. Use separate power supply or MOSFET/driver.

## Power notes
- ESP8266 runs at **3.3V**. Do **not** feed 5V into the 3.3V pin.
- NodeMCU board often has a regulator that takes VIN/USB 5V → 3.3V. That regulator has limited current (and USB supply can be limited). If your project draws >200–300 mA (Wi-Fi peaks), get a beefier 3.3V regulator or separate supply.
- ADC pin on raw ESP = 0–1.0V, but NodeMCU board exposes A0 mapped to **0–3.3V** via on-board divider. If using raw ESP module, use divider.

## Onboard LED
- Usually connected to **D4 (GPIO2)** and often **active LOW** (writing LOW turns LED ON). Remember GPIO2 must be HIGH at boot — don’t drive it low at reset.

## Common practical tips — tell it like it is
- Use **D1/D2** for I2C — saves time. Use the SPI pins for SPI devices.
- Avoid using D3/D4/D8 for devices that drive pins to the wrong level at power-up (buttons are OK if wired with correct pull resistors).
- If something isn’t booting: check boot pins (0,2,15) first. That’s the #1 rookie trap.
- For reliability with sensors/relays: use level shifting (if interfacing 5V logic) and MOSFET drivers for coils/relays.
- Expect Wi-Fi transmit spikes; don’t power servos or motors from the NodeMCU 3.3V rail.

---

Exactly — let’s break that down properly.  

Yes, **NodeMCU (ESP8266-12E/12F)** exposes **17 GPIOs total**, but not all are truly “general purpose” in practice because some double up as boot-mode or system pins.  

Here’s the **real deal** view 👇  

---

### 🧩 Total GPIO count: 17

The ESP8266 chip itself has GPIO0–GPIO16 = **17 pins**, plus a single **ADC** input.

| GPIO | NodeMCU Label | Safe to Use? | Notes / Boot Function |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| GPIO0 | D3 | ⚠️ Caution | Must be **HIGH** at boot (LOW → flash mode). Use only if you know timing. |
| GPIO1 | TX | ⚠️ Limited | UART TX; used for serial output; avoid for general I/O unless you disable serial. |
| GPIO2 | D4 | ⚠️ Caution | Must be **HIGH** at boot; also onboard LED (active LOW). |
| GPIO3 | RX | ⚠️ Limited | UART RX; used for programming; avoid unless you disable serial. |
| GPIO4 | D2 | ✅ Safe | Great for I²C (SDA). |
| GPIO5 | D1 | ✅ Safe | Great for I²C (SCL). |
| GPIO6 | — | ❌ Reserved | Used by onboard flash memory — do **not** touch. |
| GPIO7 | — | ❌ Reserved | Flash chip line. |
| GPIO8 | — | ❌ Reserved | Flash chip line. |
| GPIO9 | — | ❌ Reserved | Flash chip line. |
| GPIO10 | — | ❌ Reserved | Flash chip line. |
| GPIO11 | — | ❌ Reserved | Flash chip line. |
| GPIO12 | D6 | ✅ Safe | SPI MISO, PWM OK. |
| GPIO13 | D7 | ✅ Safe | SPI MOSI, PWM OK. |
| GPIO14 | D5 | ✅ Safe | SPI CLK, PWM OK. |
| GPIO15 | D8 | ⚠️ Caution | Must be **LOW** at boot; SPI CS default. |
| GPIO16 | D0 | ✅ Mostly | Works for digital I/O; can wake from deep sleep. No PWM or I²C. |
| ADC0  | A0 | Analog | 10-bit ADC input (0–3.3 V on NodeMCU). |

---

### ⚡ So, “usable general purpose pins” in practice

If we remove:
- Boot-critical ones (GPIO0, 2, 15)
- Serial (GPIO1, 3)
- Flash-reserved (GPIO6–10)

Then **you get about 8 fully usable GPIOs**:  
👉 **GPIO4, 5, 12, 13, 14, 16, and optionally 0 & 2 if you handle boot states carefully.**

That’s why people say *“NodeMCU has 17 GPIOs, but only 8–10 safe ones.”*

---

### 🧠 Summary: Use these for projects

| Use | Recommended Pins |
|---|---|
| **Digital I/O (safe)** | D1, D2, D5, D6, D7, D0 |
| **I²C** | D1 (SCL), D2 (SDA) |
| **SPI** | D5–D8 (SCLK, MISO, MOSI, CS) |
| **PWM/Servo** | D1, D2,

Got it — you don’t want a deep dive, just the **overall pin structure / layout summary** of NodeMCU (ESP8266), right? Here’s the clean “bird’s-eye view” version 👇  

---

## 🧩 NodeMCU (ESP8266) — Overall Pin Structure

**Total Pins (roughly):**
- **17 GPIO (General Purpose I/O)**
- **1 Analog input (A0)**
- **Power pins (3.3V, VIN, GND, etc.)**
- **Special purpose interfaces**: UART, SPI, I²C, PWM, etc.

---

### 🔹 GPIO Pins (Digital I/O)
- **Total usable GPIOs:** 17 (labeled D0–D8, plus RX/TX, and some internal ones).  
- **Actual stable usable GPIOs:** about **11–13**, because a few are reserved for boot or serial.

| Pin Range | NodeMCU Labels | Notes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Digital I/O** | D0–D8 | General purpose pins (some double as SPI/I²C/UART). |
| **Analog Input** | A0 | Reads 0–3.3V analog voltage. |
| **UART** | RX (D9), TX (D10) | Used for serial communication / programming. |
| **SPI** | D5–D8 | SPI bus (SCLK, MISO, MOSI, CS). |
| **I²C** | D1–D2 | SDA/SCL (configurable in code). |

---

### 🔹 Power & Ground
| Pin | Function |
|:--|:--|
| 3V3 | Output 3.3V regulated |
| VIN (or VU) | Input 5V (from USB or external) |
| GND | Ground |

---

### 🔹 Functional Summary
- **Total pins:** ~30 (including power, reset, EN, etc.)
- **General Purpose Pins:** 17 (digital)
- **Analog Pins:** 1
- **PWM capable:** most GPIOs
- **Communication protocols:** UART, I²C, SPI
- **Power input:** via USB or VIN (5V)
- **Logic level:** 3.3V only

---

### ⚡ Quick takeaway
> NodeMCU (ESP8266) = **17 general-purpose I/O pins**, **1 analog**, all running at **3.3V logic**, with built-in **Wi-Fi**, and supports **UART, SPI, I²C, PWM** — compact but versatile microcontroller board.

Perfect — you want the **power pin structure** (VCC, GND, 3V3, VIN, etc.) of the **NodeMCU ESP8266** board overall. Here’s the clean breakdown 👇  

---

## ⚡ **Power Pin Structure — NodeMCU ESP8266**

| **Pin Label** | **Count** | **Voltage / Function** | **Notes** |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **3V3** | 1 | 3.3 V output | Comes from onboard voltage regulator. Use to power 3.3 V sensors. |
| **VIN** (or **VU**) | 1 | 5 V input | Feeds the regulator. You can power the board from here (5 V only). Also outputs 5 V when USB is connected. |
| **GND** | 3 | Ground | Common return path for all circuits. All must be tied together. |
| **EN** (Enable) | 1 | Enable pin | Keep HIGH (3.3 V) for normal operation. Pull LOW to disable chip. |
| **RST** | 1 | Reset pin | Pull LOW to reset the ESP8266. |

---

### 🧩 So overall:
- **Power-related pins total:** **6 pins**
  - **1× VIN (5 V)**
  - **1× 3V3**
  - **3× GND**
  - **1× EN (optional, control)**  

---

### ⚠️ Quick notes:
- NodeMCU runs entirely on **3.3 V logic** — do *not* feed 5 V into 3V3 pin.  
- If you power through **VIN**, give it **5 V regulated** (can be from USB, adaptor, or external 5 V source).  
- If powering with USB, **VIN** pin outputs ~5 V — useful for external 5 V peripherals.  
- Always tie all **GNDs** together if using multiple modules/sensors.

---

So, in total:
> 🔹 **Power Pins:** 1 (VIN) + 1 (3V3) + 3 (GND) + EN + RST = **6 power/control pins**  
> 🔹 **GPIO Pins:** 17  
> 🔹 **Analog Pin:** 1
